Around 9,000 years ago, communities in the upper and lower Yangtze valleys began selecting plants whose seeds stayed attached to the stalk instead, a trait that makes harvesting far easier and is what separates a domesticated crop from its wild ancestor.

That change took centuries of repeated selection rather than a single decision, since a non-shattering plant only spreads if people keep replanting its seed. The Yangtze populations who did this were ancestral to groups later associated with Hmong-Mien and Austronesian languages, and the crop they shaped now feeds more people than any other single grain.

Sheep descend from the Asiatic mouflon and were domesticated in Mesopotamia between roughly 11,000 and 9000 BCE, before the practice spread east to Mehrgarh in the Indus Valley by about 7000 BCE. Wool was not the point at first: early flocks were kept for meat, milk and skins, the same reasons any animal got penned in rather than hunted.

Deliberate breeding for a woolly coat only shows up around 6000 BCE, and the earliest surviving woven wool cloth dates to about 4000 BCE, some two thousand years after the animals themselves were first kept. Fleece, in other words, was a slow-arriving bonus on top of an animal already valued for its meat and its milk.

Drake set out from Plymouth in December 1577 with five ships and 164 men, ostensibly bound for Alexandria to disguise a raid on Spanish territory in the Pacific. Two vessels were scuttled crossing the Atlantic, another turned back, and a captured prize was later abandoned, so only his flagship, renamed the Golden Hind, went on through the Strait of Magellan.

The Golden Hind reached Plymouth again in September 1580 with 59 men aboard, less than half the number who had left. Drake brought back looted Spanish silver and spices worth a fortune to its investors, and Elizabeth I knighted him aboard the ship the following year rather than punish an act that had infuriated Spain.

Janszoon commanded the small Dutch ship Duyfken when it charted about 320 kilometres of the Gulf of Carpentaria coast in 1606. He had no idea he had found a new continent, reading the coastline as a southward extension of New Guinea. Landing parties clashed with Aboriginal people at several points along the coast, and nine of his crew were killed before the ship turned back.

The voyage went largely unnoticed for centuries, overshadowed by the later, better-documented landings of other Dutch navigators along the same coast. Janszoon returned to a career in the Dutch East India Company's Indonesian trade rather than any further exploring, and it took historians long afterward to establish that the Duyfken, not a later ship, had made the first recorded European landing on Australian soil.

Two rival optical disc formats, backed by different groups of electronics and film companies, were heading toward a repeat of the VHS versus Betamax fight of the 1970s. Under pressure from computer and studio executives who wanted a single standard, the rivals merged their designs in 1995, and the resulting DVD format reached shops in Japan in 1996 and the United States in 1997.

A DVD held roughly seven times the data of a CD on a disc the same size, enough for a feature film with room to spare for extras and multiple language tracks. Studios also used the format to add copy protection and regional locking, restricting which country's players could read a given disc.

Nitroglycerin was powerful enough to blast through rock but unstable enough to explode from a jolt in transit, and Alfred Nobel's own brother had died in a factory accident with it. He needed a way to carry the same explosive force without carrying that risk.

In 1867 Nobel found that kieselguhr, a soft rock made of fossilised algae he sourced from the Elbe, would soak up nitroglycerin like a sponge and hold it in a stable paste that could be moulded into sticks. The result, dynamite, could be dropped, shipped and stored safely, and it detonated only when deliberately set off with a blasting cap.

Earth is estimated at about 4.54 billion years old, with an uncertainty of roughly one percent. It grew inside a flattened disc of dust and gas circling the young Sun, as smaller clumps of debris collided and stuck together in a process called accretion. Some models suggest the bulk of this assembly took only a few million years, far faster than once assumed.

The date rests on radiometric dating of meteorites and Moon rock rather than any Earth rock, since plate tectonics has recycled almost all of the original crust. The oldest surviving fragments are zircon crystals from Australia, about 4.4 billion years old, and their chemistry hints that oceans already existed soon after the crust cooled.

Before 1882, cooling a room by machine meant a fan turned by a hand crank, a foot treadle, or a belt run off a larger engine somewhere else in the building. Schuyler Wheeler, an engineer working in New York, bolted a two-bladed propeller directly onto the shaft of a small electric motor.

The result, sold under the name the 'buzz fan', needed no belt, no engine room and no operator, only a wall socket. Wheeler was twenty-two years old at the time, and the Franklin Institute awarded him its John Scott Medal for the design more than two decades later, in 1904.

In 1831 Faraday wound two insulated coils around opposite sides of an iron ring and found that switching current on in one coil briefly pushed a current through the other, even though the two wires never touched. Sliding a magnet through a simple loop of wire produced the same effect, a moving field driving current in the loop.

This was electromagnetic induction, the reverse of what his motor experiment a decade earlier had shown. Faraday went on to build a working generator from the same principle, the ancestor of the dynamos that would eventually turn mechanical motion into the electricity supplying homes and factories, though that practical shift was still decades away.

Miller Reese Hutchison built the Akouphone around a part borrowed from the telephone: a carbon transmitter, the same technology that let a voice cross a wire, repurposed to pick up sound and boost it electrically rather than rely on a simple ear trumpet's shape to gather it.

Sources differ on the exact year, placing the device anywhere from the mid to late 1890s, but agree it was among the first hearing aids to use electricity rather than acoustics alone. Hutchison later found wider fame as an engineer for Thomas Edison.

Faraday's 1821 apparatus was little more than a cup of mercury, a fixed magnet standing in it, and a wire hanging free above. Current running through the wire made it swing round and round the magnet without ever touching it, converting electrical current directly into continuous mechanical motion for the first time.

He wrote the result up and sent small working models to colleagues across Europe rather than keeping the discovery to himself. It would be decades before motors built on the same principle did useful work, but every later design, from tram engines to kitchen appliances, traces its operating idea back to that spinning wire.

Bird set its first scooters loose on the pavements of Santa Monica in September 2017 without dock stations or fixed pickup points; riders simply found one through an app, rode it, and left it wherever the trip ended. City officials in many places learned of the scheme only after scooters began appearing on their streets overnight.

Growth outpaced almost anything in the mobility industry: Bird passed ten million rides within a year and reached a billion-dollar valuation faster than any startup before it, doubling to two billion dollars by June 2018. Within roughly fourteen months it operated in more than 120 cities, and rivals like Lime rushed to copy the same dockless model before regulators caught up.

Siemens opened its Lichterfelde line near Berlin on 16 May 1881, running on track already laid to serve a Prussian military academy. Rather than string overhead wire, the two running rails themselves carried the current, one positive and one negative, the same method still used in miniature model railways today.

That arrangement worked well enough for a short suburban run but proved dangerous once the line grew busier, since a person or animal touching both rails completed the circuit. Siemens switched the route to overhead power in 1883, the configuration that became standard for the electric tramways later built across Europe and America.

In August 1914 the American Traffic Signal Company installed a red and green electric signal at the corner of East 105th Street and Euclid Avenue in Cleveland, Ohio. It was based on a design patented two years earlier by Lester Wire, a Salt Lake City policeman who had built an earlier version from a wooden box and coloured lights to save officers from directing traffic by hand.

The Cleveland signal had no amber phase and needed a police officer nearby to switch it manually between colours. A workable three colour, four way version, closer to what drivers use now, was not built until 1920, when William Potts added the amber light in Detroit to smooth the change between stop and go.

Einthoven's instrument was not a probe but a wire: a filament strung between powerful electromagnets, thin enough that the heart's own electrical current could nudge it as it passed through. A light behind the string cast its shadow onto a moving roll of photographic paper, tracing the beat as a continuous curve.

The apparatus needed water cooling, five operators and weighed around 270 kilograms, built from prototypes he had developed from 1901. It let doctors read the heart's electrical activity through skin and bone with no electrode near the organ itself, work that earned him the 1924 Nobel Prize.

William Sturgeon built his magnet from eighteen turns of bare copper wire wound around a curved iron core. Insulated wire did not exist yet, so the turns had to be spaced to keep the bare metal from touching itself and shorting the current, a fiddly limit on how strong the coil could be made.

He demonstrated the result by lifting nine pounds of iron with a seven ounce core, current from a single battery holding the load until he switched it off. Unlike a permanent magnet, his could be turned on and off at will, and that switchable pull became the working principle behind electric bells, relays and eventually electric motors.

Ørsted noticed a compass needle swing away from north whenever he closed the switch on a wire carrying current. The popular story that he stumbled onto this by chance in front of a class is a myth: he had been hunting deliberately for a link between electricity and magnetism since 1818 and published his result in 1820.

The needle did not point toward or away from the wire but curved to sit at a right angle to it, showing that a current sets up a circular magnetic field around itself. Ampere and others turned that single observation into a mathematical theory within months, and it underlies every electric motor built since.

Thomson did not call it an electron. Bending cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields in his Cambridge laboratory, he measured a charge-to-mass ratio far too large for any known atom and concluded the rays were made of something smaller, which he named a corpuscle.

He resisted the rival term for years, uneasy at physicists also talking of a positive electron, and only adopted it himself around 1914. The particle he had isolated was the first known to be smaller than an atom, undermining the idea of the atom as indivisible.

Elisha Otis designed his safety brake in 1852 while installing a freight hoist at a bedstead factory in Yonkers, New York. A toothed guide rail ran alongside the hoist car, and a spring released a catch into the teeth the instant tension on the lifting rope dropped, whether from a snapped cable or a slack line.

He proved it worked in public at the 1854 New York Crystal Palace exhibition, standing on a platform and having an assistant cut the rope holding it up. The platform fell only inches before the brake caught. Buildings taller than a few storeys, impractical while stairs were the only alternative, became sellable soon after.

Mike Brown's team at Palomar Observatory had already photographed Eris on 21 October 2003, but automated software built to spot slow-moving asteroids passed over it, since anything crawling that slowly across the sky was assumed too distant to matter. Only after finding the object Sedna did the group loosen those filters and recheck the archive, catching Eris in January 2005.

Eris turned out slightly smaller than Pluto in diameter but around a quarter more massive, massive enough that NASA briefly floated calling it a tenth planet. To settle the question, the International Astronomical Union wrote its first formal definition of a planet in August 2006, requiring it to clear its orbital neighbourhood. Neither Eris nor Pluto qualified, and both became dwarf planets.

Jesse Reno's design, which he called an inclined elevator, was little more than a continuous rubber belt studded with cast-iron cleats for grip, climbing a steep 25 degree slope with nothing resembling flat steps. He patented the mechanism in the early 1890s under the plainer name Endless Conveyor or Elevator.

Reno installed a working model at Coney Island in 1896, where fairgoers rode it purely for the novelty of standing still while a machine carried them uphill. It proved popular enough that a version was trialled for a month on the Brooklyn Bridge, years before the flat-stepped escalator familiar today replaced Reno's sloped belt entirely.

Bob Metcalfe and David Boggs built Ethernet at Xerox PARC to link the lab's new Alto computers to a shared laser printer, work that grew out of Metcalfe's study of the University of Hawaii's radio-based ALOHAnet. In a May 1973 memo, Metcalfe named the concept the Ether Network, borrowing the old physics term for a medium that was supposed to fill all of space.

The first working link ran on 11 November 1973 over shared coaxial cable at 2.94 megabits per second, using carrier sensing to let multiple machines share one line without constant collisions. Xerox never sold Ethernet as a product, but the standard it published let other companies build compatible equipment, which is how it became the wiring inside most offices.

Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were not the expedition's first attempt; a pair of climbers had turned back near the summit days earlier, exhausted. Led by Colonel John Hunt, the British party sent Hillary and Norgay up on 29 May 1953, and they reached the top at 11:30 in the morning, with Hillary cresting the final ridge slightly ahead.

News travelled by runner and coded wireless message rather than telephone: a correspondent at base camp sent word to Kathmandu using a prearranged phrase about snow conditions, so the story could break in London on the morning of Elizabeth II's coronation, 2 June. Tenzing later confirmed in his own account which of the two had stepped up first.

Edwin Hubble spent years at Mount Wilson Observatory using the 100 inch Hooker telescope, then the largest in the world, to measure distances to faint, fuzzy patches of light that most astronomers still assumed were clouds inside our own galaxy. He showed they were separate galaxies, far beyond the Milky Way.

In 1929 he combined those distances with redshift measurements gathered by Vesto Slipher and others, and found that the farther away a galaxy sat, the faster it appeared to be receding. The relationship, now called Hubble's law, gave the first observational evidence that the universe itself is expanding rather than static.

No inventor's name survives with certainty. A Dominican friar, Giordano da Pisa, told a congregation in 1306 that spectacles were less than twenty years old and that he had met the man who first made them, without recording who that was.

A Pisan friar named Alessandro della Spina is credited only with sharing the technique freely once he learned of it, and a later claim that a Florentine named Salvino degli Armati invented glasses has since been shown to be false. Venice had a spectacle makers' guild by 1320.

On 14 October 2012, Felix Baumgartner stepped out of a pressurised capsule suspended below a helium balloon at 38,969 metres, higher than any commercial jet flies, and fell for four minutes and nineteen seconds before opening his parachute. Roughly ninety minutes of ascent had preceded a free fall that lasted under five.

At the fastest point of his fall Baumgartner reached 1,357.6 kilometres per hour, or Mach 1.25, becoming the first person to break the sound barrier without a vehicle around him. The jump was part of the Red Bull Stratos project, which also tested the pressure suit and capsule design against conditions close to those of a real high-altitude bailout.

Glass fibre had been dismissed as useless for long-distance communication because signals faded within metres. In 1966, Charles Kao argued the fault lay not in the physics but in the glass itself: strip out the impurities, he calculated, and light could travel for kilometres.

Manufacturers took the claim seriously, and within a few years fibre purity improved enough to prove him right. Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work, more than four decades after a paper that most of his contemporaries had treated as an interesting but implausible bet.

Using fire and making it are two different skills with two different timelines. Charred bones deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, out of reach of any wildfire, put fire use back around 1.79 million years, well before Homo sapiens existed. The oldest strong evidence for actually starting a fire on demand is far younger: baked earth with flint and pyrite at Barnham in England, roughly 400,000 years old.

Cooking sits somewhere between the two. Heated fish teeth from a cave by the Sea of Galilee, about 780,000 years old, are among the earliest signs that food was being deliberately warmed rather than eaten raw. Some researchers push cooking back much further, to 1.8 million years, based on changes in fossil teeth, but that claim has limited support among specialists.

Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney built Computer Space as an arcade adaptation of Spacewar!, the university mainframe game they had both played as students, and Nutting Associates put it on the market in late 1971. It sold roughly 1,300 to 1,500 cabinets, turning over a million dollars, numbers Nutting had hoped a hit could beat.

The trouble was the controls. Bushnell later admitted that he and his engineer friends loved the game, but a bar patron holding a beer could not follow its rocket, gravity and shooting instructions fast enough. It did better near university campuses, and the lesson, that arcade games needed to be instantly readable, shaped Atari's Pong the following year.

Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail announced in 1992 that they had found planets not around an ordinary star but around a pulsar, PSR B1257+12, a rapidly spinning neutron star left behind by a supernova. They detected the planets by timing tiny irregularities in the pulsar's radio pulses rather than by seeing any light from the planets themselves.

It was a strange place for the first confirmed worlds beyond the solar system to turn up, since radiation from a pulsar would likely sterilise anything orbiting it. The first planet found around a normal, sun like star, 51 Pegasi b, followed in 1995, using the wobble a planet's gravity induces in its star's light.

Yuri Gagarin flew a single orbit of Earth aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961, a flight lasting 108 minutes from launch at Baikonur to landing. He held the rank of senior lieutenant when the rocket lifted off; a special order promoted him to major while he was still in flight, before he had even touched ground again.

Vostok 1 had no way to land safely with its pilot inside, so at about 7,000 metres Gagarin ejected and came down separately by parachute in a field near Saratov, startling a farmer and her daughter who found him still in his orange spacesuit. That detail briefly complicated the official record, since international rules for aviation records required a pilot to land inside the aircraft they flew.

Homo sapiens emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago from a population usually classed as Homo heidelbergensis or Homo rhodesiensis. There was no single founding moment: the change from one species to the other is a matter of gradually accumulating traits across scattered African populations, reconstructed from a handful of fossils rather than an unbroken record.

Those first populations stayed in Africa for a long stretch before spreading elsewhere. Genetic and fossil evidence points to at least two later waves leaving the continent, one around 130,000 to 100,000 years ago and a second, larger dispersal about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, during which sapiens met and sometimes interbred with other human species already settled abroad.

Ivy Mike was not a weapon so much as a factory built to prove an idea could work at all. The device, nicknamed the Sausage, weighed 82 tons and stood over 20 feet tall, housed in a corrugated aluminium shed on Elugelab Island in the Enewetak Atoll, far too large to be dropped from any aircraft.

It detonated on 1 November 1952 with a yield of 10.4 megatons, roughly 700 times the Hiroshima bomb. Elugelab disappeared entirely, replaced by an underwater crater nearly two kilometres wide, and waves up to twenty feet high stripped vegetation from neighbouring islands while radioactive debris fell on ships stationed thirty five miles away.

Leonard Thompson was fourteen years old and close to death from diabetes when doctors at Toronto General Hospital injected him with a pancreatic extract on 11 January 1922. That first dose was too impure and only gave him an allergic reaction on top of his existing illness, a discouraging start for a treatment that had looked so promising in dogs.

James Collip spent the following twelve days refining the extract, and a second course of injections beginning on 23 January brought Thompson's blood sugar down and visibly restored his strength. He lived another thirteen years on regular insulin before dying of an unrelated infection in 1935, long enough to prove that the treatment worked outside a laboratory.

No fossil marks the first living cell. The strongest direct evidence is a set of stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbial mats, found in Western Australia's Dresser Formation and dated to about 3.5 billion years ago. Some researchers argue for life as early as 4.1 billion years, based on a single zircon grain carrying a carbon signature associated with living things.

That older claim stays contested, because the same chemical signature can, in principle, form without biology at all, through volcanic or hydrothermal reactions. Even the stromatolites face the same objection from some geologists. The debate is less about whether early Earth could host life than about how confidently a single ancient rock can prove it did.

Martin Cooper made his call to needle a rival. Standing on Sixth Avenue in Manhattan on 3 April 1973, the Motorola engineer dialled Joel Engel, his counterpart at AT&T's Bell Labs, and told him he was speaking from a real handheld portable phone, a jab at Bell's competing car-phone project.

The handset was a prototype of what became the DynaTAC, 25 centimetres long and weighing over a kilogram, nicknamed the brick for its size and its single hour of talk time. Motorola would not sell a commercial version for another decade, but the call itself demonstrated that a phone could work untethered from a car or a building.

Benjamin Harris, a bookseller who had already been driven out of England once for his printing, brought out Publick Occurrences in Boston on 25 September 1690, printed by Richard Pierce on a single folded sheet. Harris meant to publish monthly, covering local news alongside reports from Europe.

There was no second issue. Colonial authorities banned the paper within four days, objecting to an unlicensed report on the treatment of French prisoners of war and to what they called reflections of a very high nature elsewhere in its pages. Massachusetts would not have another regular newspaper for fourteen years, and Harris left publishing behind for medicine.

Queen Elizabeth II opened Calder Hall in Cumberland on 17 October 1956, throwing a switch to feed power into the National Grid before a crowd of dignitaries and cameras. The ceremony was staged as proof that atomic energy had a peaceful future after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, though the site's four Magnox reactors were built chiefly to produce plutonium for Britain's weapons programme.

Electricity generation was, for years, a secondary output dressed up as the headline. Calder Hall's reactors ran on natural uranium cooled by carbon dioxide gas, a British design chosen partly because it did not depend on enriched uranium from the United States. The station stayed in service until 2003, by which time its dual purpose was long forgotten by most of the public it had once been built to reassure.

The reactor sat under the west stands of an abandoned football stadium at the University of Chicago, in a squash court, because wartime secrecy ruled out a purpose-built facility. Fermi called it plainly a crude pile of black graphite bricks and wooden timbers, stacked by hand around uranium slugs with cadmium control rods to hold the reaction in check.

On 2 December 1942 Fermi's team withdrew the rods and let the pile run for twenty-eight minutes at half a watt, roughly enough to power a light bulb, before shutting it down. Physicist Arthur Compton told a colleague by coded telephone call that the Italian navigator had landed in the New World and found the natives friendly, confirming the chain reaction had worked without naming it.

Ronald and Richard Herrick were identical twins, which mattered more than any surgical skill: a kidney moved between genetically identical bodies would not be rejected, a problem that had defeated every earlier attempt at transplantation. On 23 December 1954 at Boston's Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, Joseph Murray and J. Hartwell Harrison carried out the five and a half hour operation.

Richard, the recipient, lived another eight years, long enough to marry and have two children, before dying of an unrelated heart condition rather than organ failure. Ronald, the donor, lived more than fifty years afterward with no lasting harm, and Murray later won a Nobel Prize for showing that transplantation could work at all.

On 1 January 1914 the pilot Tony Jannus flew a wooden Benoist flying boat across Tampa Bay, a 23 mile hop that rarely climbed above five feet over the water. The passenger seat had been auctioned off the night before for 400 dollars, won by Abram Pheil, a former mayor of St Petersburg who beat out the other bidders for the honour of going first.

The flight took about twenty three minutes, roughly what the same trip by rail or steamer took hours to cover. A one way ticket normally cost five dollars, and the St Petersburg Tampa Airboat Line kept running two flights a day for a few months before the novelty and the funding both ran out.

Bell Labs researchers Calvin Fuller, Daryl Chapin and Gerald Pearson were not looking for a way to power satellites when they refined silicon doping in 1954; Chapin was trying to build a reliable power source for remote telephone equipment in humid climates where batteries corroded quickly.

Their silicon cell was the first that converted a practical fraction of sunlight into usable electrical current rather than a laboratory curiosity, and Bell Labs demonstrated it publicly the same year to newspapers who called it a battery that ran on sunlight. It would take the space programme, not the telephone network, to make the technology worth its cost.

American and British intelligence had assumed the Soviet Union was years from a bomb, not months. RDS-1 was detonated at the Semipalatinsk test site in Kazakhstan on 29 August 1949, a near copy of the American Fat Man design built on details passed by wartime espionage, with a yield of about 22 kilotons.

A US Air Force weather aircraft flying a routine sampling route collected radioactive debris on 3 September, and analysis confirmed a nuclear blast rather than a reactor accident. Truman announced the finding publicly on 23 September; Soviet media hinted at construction work before admitting nothing directly, while Washington accelerated its own hydrogen bomb programme in response.

Columbia lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on 12 April 1981 carrying John Young, on his fifth spaceflight, and rookie pilot Robert Crippen. It was the first crewed American launch since the Apollo-Soyuz mission six years earlier, and the first time a spacecraft designed to fly again was tested with astronauts aboard rather than unmanned first.

Over two days and thirty-six orbits, the crew put the untested orbiter through its paces before gliding it to a runway landing in California, something no previous American spacecraft had done. Engineers later counted roughly seventy anomalies from the flight, none serious enough to stop the shuttle programme running for three more decades.

Dennis Tito, an American engineer and investment manager, launched aboard Soyuz TM-32 on 28 April 2001 after paying a reported twenty million dollars for the seat, a deal NASA had initially opposed and only accepted after months of negotiation with the Russian space agency. He spent just under eight days in orbit, most of it aboard the International Space Station.

Tito trained for months in Star City outside Moscow alongside professional cosmonauts to qualify for the flight, and he orbited the Earth 128 times before landing. His trip opened a market that Russia continued selling seats into for the next decade, before the practice paused once the space shuttle retired and Soyuz seats became scarce.

Nyayanga in Kenya has yielded the oldest confirmed stone tool industry, the Oldowan, dated to about 2.9 million years ago, with a possibly distinct and even older set of tools from Lomekwi at roughly 3.3 million years. Nobody knows for certain which species made them. At Nyayanga the flakes turned up alongside butchered hippo bones, and beside teeth from Paranthropus rather than any Homo species.

That ambiguity matters, because the tools have long been credited to a single toolmaking lineage leading to us. Cut marked bones found with tools at Gona in Ethiopia, about 2.6 million years old, show the same basic technique was already spread across East Africa, used for stripping meat and marrow rather than shaping anything ornamental.

Twenty three Jewish refugees from Dutch Brazil landed in New Amsterdam in September 1654 and were grudgingly allowed to settle a year later. For decades their congregation, Shearith Israel, worshipped in rented rooms rather than a public building of its own.

That changed on Mill Street in lower Manhattan in 1730, when the congregation dedicated its first purpose built synagogue. It remained the only synagogue in New York City for nearly a century, and Shearith Israel is still counted the oldest Jewish congregation in the country.

The Constitution required a headcount every ten years to divide seats in Congress fairly among the states, and the first count ran through August 1790. There was no census bureau yet: federal marshals rode out through their judicial districts asking each household how many people lived there, under Thomas Jefferson's direction as secretary of state.

The tally came to 3,929,214 people across thirteen states and the Southwest Territory, with Virginia the largest and Delaware the smallest. The categories counted were blunt by later standards, splitting households only into free persons, other free persons, and enslaved people, a structure that shaped political representation for decades.

The Endeavour left Plymouth on 26 August 1768 with a cover story and a secret. Its stated task was to carry astronomers to Tahiti to watch Venus cross the sun, a measurement meant to fix the distance from Earth to the sun; sealed orders told Cook to search further for a rumoured southern continent once that was done.

Joseph Banks, a wealthy botanist, paid to bring his own team of naturalists and artists aboard, and the ship later picked up Tupaia, a Tahitian navigator whose knowledge of Pacific sailing and languages proved as valuable as any instrument on board. Cook was forty and had never commanded an ocean voyage of this length before.

Before Vostok 6, Valentina Tereshkova worked in a textile factory and kept a secret hobby from her family: competitive parachuting, which was exactly what caught the Soviet space programme's attention. On 16 June 1963 she flew solo, orbiting Earth 48 times over nearly three days.

She was 26, and remains the youngest woman ever to fly in space. No other woman flew alone again; every later female cosmonaut and astronaut has flown as part of a crew. Tereshkova's callsign, Chaika, meaning seagull, became one of the more famous words radioed home from orbit.

Hattie Caraway of Arkansas was appointed to the Senate on the death of her husband, Senator Thaddeus Caraway, in December 1931, in a period when such appointments were widely treated as caretaker roles for a widow. She then stood for the seat outright in a special election in January 1932 and won it.

Nicknamed Silent Hattie for rarely speaking on the floor, she went on to win a full term later that year with unexpected backing from Louisiana's Huey Long, becoming the first woman to serve a full Senate term and, in 1933, the first to chair a Senate committee. She served until losing the 1944 primary to J. William Fulbright.

Bone and shell hooks from around this period, curved and often barbed, mark a shift away from spearing or netting fish toward a method that let one person tend a line while doing other work. The earliest examples come from coastal and river sites where fish bones pile up in the same layers, showing the tool was put to immediate use rather than made and left idle.

A hook opened up deep water and fast-moving fish that spears and nets struggled to reach, adding a food source that did not compete with land game for the same hunting grounds. That flexibility mattered most in lean seasons, when a failed hunt on land could be offset by whatever a line pulled out of the water.

IBM did not build the floppy disk to move files between machines, which is what it later became famous for. Engineers Warren Dalziel, Jay Brent Nilson and Ralph Flores designed the 8 inch disk, shipped as the 23FD in 1971, to solve a narrower problem: loading microprogram code into a mainframe's control store at startup, a job that needed something cheap, replaceable and read only.

That first disk held 80 kilobytes. When IBM's 33FD followed in 1973 with a read and write head, the same format could hold nearly 250 kilobytes, and other manufacturers adopted it because it was already standardised hardware rather than a proprietary format they would have had to license.

Earlier flush toilets, including a design John Harington had built two centuries before, solved waste removal but left an open pipe running straight back to the sewer, and the smell followed it into the house. Cumming, a watchmaker and instrument maker by trade rather than a plumber, bent the outlet pipe into an S shape.

Water settled permanently in the curve of that S and blocked the gases behind it, which is still how a toilet trap works today. His 1775 patent also linked the inlet valve to the flush handle so a single pull both emptied the bowl and refilled it, a mechanism closer to a clockmaker's linkage than a builder's fitting.

A griffon vulture's wing bone has two hollow segments naturally suited to a pipe, and whoever carved this one in the Hohle Fels cave near Ulm, Germany, notched five finger holes and a V-shaped mouthpiece into it. Archaeologists pulled the fragments out in 2008 and dated the layer to roughly 42,000 years ago, close to when modern humans first reached the region.

The find was published in Nature in 2009 alongside other Aurignacian-era pipes from nearby Swabian caves, and beside it lay the Venus of Hohle Fels, an ivory figurine from the same layer. Together they suggest music and figurative art arrived as a package with the first modern humans in Europe, not as something invented centuries later.

Qesem Cave in Israel was occupied from roughly 420,000 to 220,000 years ago, and among the bones left there archaeologists found deer leg bones kept intact, with the skin left on, for weeks after the animal was killed rather than cracked open right away. Marrow inside a covered bone stays edible far longer than exposed meat, and the delay only makes sense if it was deliberate.

Breaking the bones open later took a dedicated tool: shaped stone hammerstones found at the site match wear patterns from splitting large bones specifically to reach the marrow inside. Together the intact bones and the purpose-made hammerstones describe a stored larder, not a single meal, which pushes the deliberate management of a food supply back further than most other evidence allows.

Before October 1913, building a Model T chassis at Ford's Highland Park plant took a team roughly twelve and a half hours, working around a stationary car. Henry Ford's engineers instead kept the car moving past stationary workers on a conveyor line, each person repeating one task rather than assembling a whole vehicle.

By 1914 the same chassis took ninety three minutes. The saved labour let Ford cut the Model T's price from 825 dollars in 1909 to 440 dollars in 1914, and to 265 dollars a decade later, turning a car built for the wealthy into one his own factory workers could plausibly buy.

Léon Foucault first showed his pendulum at the Paris Observatory in February 1851, then built a larger version for the public: a 28 kilogram bob on a 67 metre wire hung from the dome of the Panthéon. Visitors watched it knock over small pegs arranged in a ring on the floor.

The pendulum's swing plane appeared to rotate over the course of the day, completing a full turn in roughly thirty two hours at that latitude. The bob itself kept swinging in a fixed direction in space; it was the floor beneath it, and the whole building, that was turning with the Earth.

Lewis Waterman is often said to have invented the modern fountain pen after an ink blot ruined a contract he was trying to sell, costing him the deal and pushing him into pen design out of spite. That story is untrue: he had already taken over a small pen business the year before his first patent.

What he actually solved, in a patent granted in 1884, was the air problem rather than the ink problem. Earlier pens let air back into the reservoir in one uncontrolled gulp, forcing ink out in a flood; Waterman's three-channel feed let air in and ink out at the same steady rate, so the pen wrote without flooding or starving.

No bolt struck the kite. What the popular version leaves out is that Benjamin Franklin's kite drew a charge simply by flying near a storm cloud in June 1752, with his son William holding the line beside him. Franklin noticed loose threads on the string standing apart from each other, the sign that it had become charged.

He touched a key tied to the string and drew a spark, then used the charge to fill a Leyden jar. The fullest account of the day comes not from Franklin himself, who never gave precise details of his own experiment, but from Joseph Priestley's history written fifteen years later from what Franklin had told him.

John Walker was mixing chemicals in his shop when a dried lump of his paste, scraped off a stick against his hearth to clean it, burst into flame. He had been trying to make a percussion powder for guns and stumbled onto something else entirely: a stick that lit itself with friction.

He never patented the friction match. Asked why, he said only that he expected it to benefit the public, so people should simply have it. He kept no written record of the exact formula either, and within a few years a chemist named Samuel Jones had copied the idea and sold his own version as the Lucifer match, far more successfully than Walker ever did.

Clarence Birdseye got the idea in Labrador between 1912 and 1915, watching Inuit fishermen pull fish from the ice that had frozen almost instantly in the brutal cold and still tasted fresh when thawed months later. Slow commercial freezing, by contrast, formed large ice crystals that ruptured cells and left food mushy.

In 1930 his company tested the resulting quick-frozen method commercially, stocking eighteen retail stores around Springfield, Massachusetts with 26 frozen items, from peas to fish fillets. The trial is generally treated as the start of retail frozen food, though home freezers common enough to store it widely were still years away.

At Qafzeh Cave in what is now Israel, human skeletons roughly 100,000 years old were found with red ochre concentrated only around the bones, not scattered generally through the cave sediment. That pattern is the evidence: ochre placed with a body and nowhere else implies a deliberate act at the time of burial, not a coincidence of geology.

Before Qafzeh, most researchers dated the first symbolic behaviour in humans to around 50,000 years ago. A burial with pigment pushed that back by tens of thousands of years, and it remains one of the earliest sites cited whenever the question is not whether a body was buried, but whether it was buried with any meaning attached.

On 7 January 1610 Galileo pointed his telescope at Jupiter and noted three small points of light near it, which he first took for fixed stars. Watching them shift position over the following nights, he realised a fourth had joined them and that all four were circling the planet rather than sitting still against the sky.

He named them the Medicean stars after his patron Cosimo de' Medici; they are now called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Their existence mattered beyond the discovery itself: if moons could orbit a body other than Earth, the old argument that everything in the heavens must circle Earth alone no longer held, and Copernicus's sun-centred model gained a hard piece of evidence.

Nintendo released the Game Boy in Japan on 21 April 1989, designed by Gunpei Yokoi under a philosophy he called lateral thinking with withered technology: use cheap, already-obsolete parts cleverly rather than chase the newest chips. Its dim green screen and monophonic speaker looked unimpressive next to rival handhelds with colour displays.

Bundling it with Tetris in North America and Europe turned out to matter more than the hardware. Nintendo judged the puzzle game would appeal well beyond the young boys who bought Super Mario Land, and by the line's discontinuation in 2003 it had sold nearly 119 million units, still the best-selling handheld family for years afterward.

Garibaldi sailed from Genoa on 5 May 1860 with barely more than a thousand volunteers, most of them armed with ageing muskets and no artillery to speak of, against a Bourbon kingdom with a standing army many times their size. Recruits joined as the force moved through Sicily, swelling it far beyond its starting number.

By October the expedition had taken Sicily and Naples, and Garibaldi styled himself dictator of the south only in the king's name. He met Victor Emmanuel II at Teano and handed the conquered territories over to him rather than keeping power himself, clearing the way for the Kingdom of Italy to be proclaimed the following March.

William Murdoch worked for the steam engine firm Boulton and Watt, experimenting on the side with gas produced by heating coal in a sealed retort. In 1792 he piped the gas through his own house in Redruth, Cornwall, and lit it, the first home known to be illuminated this way.

The demonstration stayed a curiosity for years before Murdoch scaled it up: by 1798 he was lighting the main building of the Soho Foundry, and in 1802 he lit its exterior in a public display bright enough to draw crowds. Within a couple of decades gas lighting was ordinary in British streets and factories.

Richard Gatling built his gun in 1861 not to kill more efficiently but, he said later, to reduce the size of armies. Most Civil War deaths came from disease spread through crowded camps, and Gatling reasoned that a single crew turning a hand crank could do the work of a hundred riflemen and let fewer men be exposed to it.

Six barrels rotated around a central shaft, each firing and reloading in turn as the crank turned, so the gun kept firing far faster than any rifle could be reloaded by hand. The design saw little use in the war it was built for and only entered wide military service afterward, well before Gatling later adapted it to an electric motor.

Einstein presented the finished field equations to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin in November 1915, capping eight years of work that began with a thought about a man falling freely from a roof feeling weightless. The theory replaced Newton's idea of gravity as a force with the idea that mass bends the space and time around it, and that objects simply follow the curves.

The first hard test came in 1919, when Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the darkened sun during a solar eclipse and found their light bent by almost exactly the amount Einstein had predicted. Newspapers reported the result as proof that a new universe had replaced the old one, and Einstein went from a respected physicist to a household name almost overnight.

The Trades Union Congress called a general strike on 4 May 1926 after mine owners announced longer hours and lower wages for coal miners, and roughly one and a half million transport, print and heavy industry workers walked out in support. Volunteers, students and soldiers kept buses running and unloaded ships while the government treated the standoff as a direct challenge to its authority.

The TUC called the strike off on 12 May without securing any guarantee against victimisation of strikers or improvement in the miners' terms, a decision many rank and file workers saw as a betrayal. The miners alone stayed out for months longer, but hunger eventually forced most of them back into the pits on the owners' original terms of longer hours for less pay.

Eisenhower, Soviet premier Nikolai Bulganin, Britain's Anthony Eden and France's Edgar Faure sat down on 18 July 1955, the first time leaders of the wartime allies had met as a group since Potsdam a decade earlier. Nikita Khrushchev, not yet the Soviet Union's formal head of state, attended alongside Bulganin and was already clearly the more powerful figure in the room.

Eisenhower's main proposal, Open Skies, offered to let each side fly reconnaissance aircraft over the other's territory to guard against a surprise attack. The Soviets rejected it as an espionage scheme, and the summit produced no binding agreement on arms or Germany, though the cordial atmosphere itself became known afterward as the Geneva spirit.

Fuller did not invent the geodesic dome; Walther Bauersfeld had already built one for a planetarium at the Carl Zeiss works in Jena, Germany, which opened to the public in 1926. What Fuller did, working with the artist Kenneth Snelson at Black Mountain College in 1948, was coin the term geodesic and popularise the structure as an efficient, mass-producible building form.

Its strength comes from triangular panels that spread stress evenly across the whole shell, letting a geodesic dome enclose more space with less material than almost any other shape. Fuller patented his version in 1954 and hoped it would solve postwar housing shortages; instead it found its niche in exhibition halls, radar stations and, decades later, Epcot's Spaceship Earth.

The machine at IBM's New York headquarters on 7 January 1954 knew only six grammar rules and 250 words, all drawn from organic chemistry and a scattering of political phrases. Even so, it converted more than sixty Romanised Russian sentences into English, and reporters treated the demonstration as proof that language itself had been cracked.

The Georgetown researchers told journalists that machine translation could be a solved problem within three to five years. It was not: a 1966 government report found a decade of funded research had failed to deliver working general translation, and US funding for the field collapsed soon after, decades before the demonstration's optimism was earned.

Doctors for centuries had blamed disease on bad air rising from swamps and waste. Louis Pasteur's work from the late 1850s onward, showing that broth left sealed against airborne microbes stayed sterile indefinitely, undercut the idea that decay and disease simply generated themselves from within.

Robert Koch pushed the case from correlation to proof, isolating the bacterium behind anthrax and setting out criteria, published in 1884, for showing that one specific microbe caused one specific disease. Together their findings displaced miasma theory over the 1880s and gave doctors a reason to sterilise instruments rather than merely ventilate a ward.

On 16 March 1926, in a cabbage field belonging to his aunt in Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launched a spindly rocket fuelled by gasoline and liquid oxygen, the first flight of its kind. According to his own diary the rocket climbed 41 feet and travelled 184 feet in about two and a half seconds before the lower half of its nozzle burned away.

It was a modest flight by any later standard, roughly the height of a small tree, but it proved that liquid propellants could actually lift a rocket rather than just burn in a lab setup. Goddard kept the work largely to himself after early press mockery, and the rocket he later nicknamed Nell is now commemorated at the site as a National Historic Landmark.

Gorillas were not unknown to the people who lived alongside them, but Western science had no formal description until 1847, when American missionary physician Thomas Savage and naturalist Jeffries Wyman examined skulls and bones from near the Gabon River and published the first scientific account.

They named the species Troglodytes gorilla, initially grouping it with chimpanzees in the same genus. Savage had never seen a living gorilla; his description relied entirely on skeletal remains and secondhand accounts from local hunters, which left the animal's size and temperament wildly exaggerated in the following decades.

Navstar 1 rode an Atlas rocket, a converted intercontinental ballistic missile, out of Vandenberg Air Force Base on 22 February 1978. It was a prototype, one of ten Block I satellites Rockwell built to prove the concept rather than serve the public, and the network would not be declared fully operational for another seventeen years.

The satellites broadcast on two frequencies, 1575.42 and 1227.60 megahertz, powered by solar panels charging nickel cadmium batteries through the hours spent in Earth's shadow. Designed to last five years, the final Block I satellite kept working until November 1995, long enough to see its civilian descendants guiding phones and cars rather than missile guidance systems.

At 9:50:45 UTC on 14 September 2015, both LIGO detectors, separated by 3,000 kilometres in Louisiana and Washington State, registered an identical chirp lasting a fraction of a second. It came from two black holes, 36 and 29 times the mass of the Sun, spiralling together and merging 1.4 billion light years away; the collision converted three solar masses into gravitational wave energy in an instant.

Einstein had predicted such waves in 1916 but doubted they could ever be measured, since they stretch space by less than the width of a proton over the length of LIGO's arms. Scientists spent five months verifying the signal before announcing it on 11 February 2016, a full century after the prediction was first written down.

Gottfried Kirch spotted the comet from Coburg on 14 November 1680, the first comet ever found using a telescope rather than the naked eye. It grew bright enough to see in daylight and trailed a tail long enough to alarm observers across Europe, swinging so close to the sun that it passed within about 930,000 kilometres of its surface before swinging back out.

Isaac Newton used tracking data on the comet's path to test Kepler's laws and to argue that comets, like planets, obey gravity rather than moving unpredictably, work that fed directly into the Principia seven years later. In Mexico, the Jesuit astronomer Eusebio Kino published his own account of its course, one of the earliest scientific treatises printed anywhere in the Americas.

Flaking a stone chips off sharp fragments by striking it; grinding does the opposite, wearing a coarse-grained rock like basalt or granite down slowly against another stone, often with sand and water as an abrasive, until it takes on a smooth, durable working surface rather than a cutting edge.

The technique is usually associated with the much later Neolithic, when it produced axes and quern stones for farming communities. Japan is the exception: ground stone tools there predate that broader Neolithic adoption by an estimated 25,000 years, and the Levant's Natufian sites show the same shift happening independently during the Mesolithic.

The Wujing Zongyao took a team of Song dynasty scholars five years to compile, led by the official Zeng Gongliang with an astronomer and a court scholar assisting him. Commissioned under Emperor Renzong partly because of conflict with the Western Xia, it covered naval vessels and siege engines alongside its chemistry.

It sets down not one formula but three: a fireball for trebuchets, a caltrop bomb built to snag on wooden structures, and a poisonous smoke ball for chemical attacks. Each mixed saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal with additives like pitch and wax, and the saltpetre content already varied between roughly a third and three fifths by weight.

Taoist alchemists were not looking for a weapon. They were mixing sulphur, charcoal and saltpetre in search of an elixir that would grant eternal life, following methods described as early as the second century by the alchemist Wei Boyang, who warned that some such powders could flare and dance violently.

The Chinese name that stuck, huoyao, translates as fire medicine, a label that still carries the trace of that original purpose. Historians note that the strong link drawn between gunpowder and Taoism may partly reflect which texts happened to survive rather than who actually did the mixing.

Fritz Haber's first working apparatus, built in 1909 with his assistant Robert Le Rossignol, produced ammonia one drop at a time, roughly a cupful an hour, by forcing nitrogen and hydrogen together under high pressure and heat over a metal catalyst. It was a laboratory curiosity until BASF bought the rights and set Carl Bosch the job of scaling it a thousandfold.

Bosch solved the engineering problem within a year, and BASF's Oppau plant was making twenty tonnes of ammonia a day by 1914, feeding a fertiliser industry that no longer depended on mined nitrate. One later estimate holds that without this synthetic nitrogen, the world's cropland could not have fed even half of the population alive by 2000.

At Kathu Pan in South Africa, stone points around 500,000 years old show damage patterns matching a spear tip rather than a hand-held blade, the earliest solid evidence that toolmakers were binding stone to wood. Hafting turns a single sharp edge into a compound tool: the same point thrown or thrust with a shaft's leverage does far more damage than the stone alone ever could.

Making a hafted spear demands planning several steps ahead: shaping the point, preparing a shaft, and finding a binding, whether sinew, plant fibre or an early adhesive, that will hold under impact. That sequence of foresight is why some researchers treat hafting as evidence for a real jump in working memory among the common ancestors of humans and Neanderthals, not just a better weapon.

Hanno led a Carthaginian fleet, said to number sixty ships, out through the Strait of Gibraltar and down the West African coast, founding settlements along the way. His own account, the Periplus, survives only as an abbreviated Greek translation of the lost Punic original, describing rivers, nomadic tribes and a night sky lit by distant fires.

How far south he got is disputed: estimates range from southern Morocco to as far as Gabon, because the sailing distances he recorded do not match any single coastline well. He also described an island of hairy, aggressive people his interpreters called gorillas, a name later borrowed for the modern ape.

A harpoon is not just a sharpened spear. Its head is barbed and often detachable, designed to twist sideways once inside an animal so the shaft can pull free while a line stays fixed in the wound, which lets a hunter tire a large or slippery target rather than relying on one clean strike.

The earliest known examples, bone points from Katanda in the Democratic Republic of Congo, were most likely used to spear catfish and are estimated at around 90,000 years old, though dating methods for material that old carry real uncertainty. Far later, cave art at Cosquer in southern France shows the same idea applied to seals.

Silcrete, a common local stone, flakes poorly straight out of the ground but turns glassy and easy to work if it is buried in sand and heated slowly under a controlled fire, then left to cool before knapping. At Pinnacle Point on South Africa's southern coast, archaeologists found the oldest known evidence of people doing exactly this.

The technique demanded fire management well beyond cooking: a steady, moderated heat over hours, not a quick blaze. Because it turns up this early, it counts against the older idea that complex, planned toolmaking only appeared with a sudden behavioural shift around 40,000 years ago, and points instead to a slower build-up of skill.

In 1927 Werner Heisenberg proposed a limit that has nothing to do with clumsy instruments: no measurement, however good, can pin down a particle's position and momentum at once beyond a fixed mathematical bound. Improve one figure and the other necessarily blurs, a trade-off built into quantum mechanics itself rather than a gap that better engineering could close.

Heisenberg worked out the idea while at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, at only twenty-five years old. The relation is written as a simple inequality involving Planck's constant, and it became a central statement of the new quantum theory, alongside Bohr's complementarity and Schrodinger's wave equation.

Sikorsky's VS-300 first left the ground on a tether on 14 September 1939, its inventor at the controls. Earlier helicopters had used paired or stacked rotors to cancel torque; Sikorsky instead fitted a single main rotor with a small vertical tail rotor, a configuration copied by nearly every helicopter built since.

The machine flew untethered for the first time on 13 May 1940 and, fitted with floats, became the first practical amphibious helicopter in April 1941. The following month it stayed airborne for one hour, thirty-two minutes and twenty-six seconds, breaking a German endurance record. It now sits in the Henry Ford Museum in Michigan.

Hero of Alexandria's aeolipile was a sealed sphere mounted over a fire, with two bent nozzles that let escaping steam spin it on its axis. It is the earliest steam turbine on record, built in the first century AD, and it worked exactly as described: heat water, trap the steam, let it push against the air through an angled outlet.

It never became a machine that pulled a load or turned a mill. Rome had cheap labour, no market demanding mechanised output, and metalworking that could not yet hold higher pressures safely, so the aeolipile stayed a lecture-hall demonstration of a principle rather than the start of an industrial engine.

Herodotus set out to record the Greco-Persian Wars before, in his own words, time erased the memory of what both Greeks and non-Greeks had achieved. Nothing in the resulting text can be dated later than about 430 BC, and the work is the earliest surviving Greek prose narrative on this scale, which is why Cicero later called him the father of history.

Not everyone agreed the title was earned. Thucydides, writing soon after, dismissed him as a mere storyteller, and later critics went further, branding him the father of lies for including folk tales and secondhand travellers' reports alongside verified events. Modern historians still read him as part reporter and part collector of good stories.

Heinrich Hertz built his transmitter from two brass rods with a spark gap between them, powered by a induction coil throwing off roughly 30,000 volts, and a separate loop of wire to detect the waves it sent across his Karlsruhe laboratory. The sparks jumping the receiving gap confirmed that James Clerk Maxwell's predicted electromagnetic waves were real.

Asked what use his discovery might have, Hertz reportedly answered that it was of no use whatsoever, just an experiment proving Maxwell right. He died in 1894, aged 36, without living to see Guglielmo Marconi turn the same waves into wireless telegraphy within a decade, or radio into a global industry within his own century.

Heyerdahl was trying to prove a specific and, it turned out, wrong idea: that Polynesia had been settled by seafarers from South America rather than from Southeast Asia. To show the voyage was physically possible with pre-Columbian technology, he built a balsa-log raft named Kon-Tiki and set out from Callao, Peru, on 28 April 1947 with five companions.

The raft drifted 6,900 kilometres across the Pacific on ocean currents and trade winds, reaching a reef off the Raroia atoll after 101 days at sea. The crossing became a bestselling book and film, but genetic and archaeological evidence has since confirmed Polynesians descended from Southeast Asian populations who migrated east, not the other way round.

No garment from this period survives, since hide decomposes almost as fast as the animal it came from. What does survive are the tools used to work it: stone scrapers from African sites several hundred thousand years old carry wear patterns matching the repeated, angled strokes needed to remove flesh and fat from a skin, rather than the marks left by cutting meat or wood.

Turning a raw hide into something wearable or weatherproof takes real processing: scraping it clean, working it to keep it supple as it dries, and sometimes smoking it, or it stiffens into something closer to a board than fabric. That chain of steps, inferred from the scrapers rather than any surviving hide, is the basis for placing organised clothing and simple shelter coverings this far back.

Earlier scholars had assumed Egyptian hieroglyphs were purely symbolic, each sign standing for an idea rather than a sound. Champollion's breakthrough was to treat the royal names ringed in cartouches, Ptolemy and Cleopatra among them, as phonetic spellings and match their sounds letter by letter against the Greek text alongside them on the Rosetta Stone.

On 14 September 1822, comparing Coptic with a hieroglyphic sign for 'birth' in a text from Abu Simbel, he confirmed the system worked the same way throughout. He is said to have run to his brother's office shouting that he had it, then collapsed. He published the decipherment on 27 September 1822.

On 4 July 2012, physicists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced a new particle weighing around 133 times a proton's mass, found independently by the ATLAS and CMS detectors. Peter Higgs had proposed the underlying field in 1964, one of six theorists who reached similar conclusions that year, but the mechanism carries only his name because his 1966 paper worked out how the particle itself would decay.

The Higgs field explains why particles have mass at all: without it, electrons and quarks would move at light speed and no atom could hold together. Higgs, then 83, watched the announcement from the audience in Geneva and shared the following year's Nobel Prize in Physics with Francois Englert, whose independent 1964 paper reached the same conclusion.

Almost nothing about Hippocrates's own life is reliably documented beyond his birth around 460 BC on the island of Kos. What survives of his reputation rests on an idea rather than a biography: that illness came from environment, diet and daily habits, not divine punishment, and could therefore be studied and treated by observation.

The seventy or so treatises known as the Hippocratic Corpus are not confidently his own writing. Most scholars think they were produced by later students and physicians working in his tradition, and later collected and attributed to him as his fame grew, possibly when librarians in Alexandria filed assorted medical texts under his name.

The US Centers for Disease Control had already been tracking a mysterious cluster of illnesses in gay men since 1981 before anyone knew what was causing it. In 1983 a team at the Institut Pasteur in Paris, led by Luc Montagnier, isolated a retrovirus from a patient's lymph node and named it LAV, the first time the agent behind the syndrome had been captured and grown in a lab.

A separate American laboratory led by Robert Gallo announced its own isolation the following year, and the two groups' claims to priority became a long, bitter dispute over credit and patent royalties on the antibody test. The virus was renamed HIV in 1986, and testing blood for it began reshaping transfusion and public health practice almost immediately.

A 2.04 million year old skull from Drimolen in South Africa is the oldest specimen currently assigned to Homo erectus, though most fossils date closer to 1 to 1.8 million years. Within a few hundred thousand years the species had reached Georgia, Indonesia and China, the first hominin known to leave Africa at all, well before modern humans existed.

Fire is harder to pin on it than the old textbook image suggests. Burnt material at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa is 1.7 million years old, but controlled, everyday fire use does not become common in the archaeological record until 300,000 to 400,000 years ago, long after Homo erectus had spread across three continents. Its Acheulean handaxes, by contrast, are unmistakably its own invention.

Hooke was not looking at anything alive. He sliced a thin sheet of cork and put it under his microscope for a 1665 book called Micrographia, and found the dead tissue was built from tiny walled compartments, packed together with no gaps between them.

The shape reminded him of a monk's dormitory or a honeycomb, so he called the compartments cells, a name that stuck long after biologists worked out what was actually inside living ones. Micrographia's engravings, some folding out larger than the book itself, made his tiny discovery visible to readers who had never looked through a lens.

A horseshoe complete with its nails turned up in the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai, in modern Belgium, dated to the fifth century. Roman writers had described mule shoes centuries earlier, but those were probably hipposandals, leather boots strapped over the hoof rather than iron nailed to it.

Written references to horseshoes are scarcer than the metal itself. The earliest clear mention of crescent shaped irons and their nails dates to 910, and only becomes common in texts after that. On rocky or icy ground a shod horse kept its footing and its hoof wall intact where an unshod one wore down or split.

A sheep, a duck and a rooster went first, sent up over Versailles in September 1783 before Louis XVI to check whether altitude itself was survivable. Two months later, on 21 November, Pilatre de Rozier and the marquis d'Arlandes climbed into a basket beneath a Montgolfier balloon at the Chateau de la Muette and cut loose.

They rose to roughly 900 metres and drifted about nine kilometres across Paris in twenty five minutes, close enough to fires drifting up from the straw-fed burner that embers kept scorching the fabric and Pilatre had to beat them out with a wet sponge. There was fuel left for four or five times the distance when they set the balloon down between two windmills.

Working at Mount Wilson Observatory in 1923 and 1924, Edwin Hubble photographed a faint star inside the Andromeda nebula and recognised it as a Cepheid, a type of star whose brightness pulses in a rhythm that reveals its true distance. The distance he calculated put Andromeda far beyond the edge of the Milky Way, which astronomers had assumed held everything that existed.

Hubble announced the result at a scientific meeting on New Year's Day 1925, and it overturned the reigning view that the Milky Way was the entire universe. What had been catalogued as fuzzy nebulae turned out to be separate galaxies of their own, each holding billions of stars, and the observable universe suddenly became almost unimaginably larger than anyone had supposed.

Space Shuttle Discovery carried Hubble into orbit on 24 April 1990, deploying it the next day after decades of delay, including the years lost grounding the shuttle fleet after Challenger. Within weeks the images coming back were blurred, and engineers traced the fault to the primary mirror's edge, ground too flat by roughly 2,200 nanometres.

Rather than bring the telescope home, NASA sent astronauts to fit it with corrective optics, nicknamed spectacles, during a December 1993 servicing mission that cost about 500 million dollars. The repair worked, and the sharpened images that followed helped justify keeping Hubble flying for decades rather than writing it off as a costly failure.

Hired by the Dutch East India Company to find a northeast route to Asia, Henry Hudson instead turned his ship the Halve Maen west across the Atlantic in 1609 and sailed up the river that now bears his name, reaching roughly as far as present-day Albany before shallow water stopped him. It was, again, not the passage he had been sent to find.

The voyage gave the Dutch their claim to the region and led directly to the colony of New Netherland. Hudson himself did not live to see it: on a later expedition seeking a northwest passage, his crew mutinied in 1611 and set him, his son and seven others adrift in a small boat in the bay that also carries his name. None of them was ever seen again.

Humboldt sailed from La Coruna in June 1799 with the botanist Aime Bonpland, funding the whole venture from his own inheritance. In Venezuela the pair paddled the Orinoco and confirmed a natural channel, the Casiquiare, linking that river's basin to the Amazon's, a connection earlier travellers had doubted existed.

In 1802 they climbed Chimborazo in Ecuador, reaching roughly 5,878 metres before ice and altitude turned them back, then the highest a European had gone. Humboldt's real haul was data: barometric readings, plant collections and notes on colonial economies that took decades to publish and reshaped how geography itself was studied.

Other chemists had produced hydrogen gas before Henry Cavendish, including Robert Boyle a century earlier, but nobody had shown it was a distinct substance rather than a variant of ordinary air. Cavendish generated it by dripping acid onto metals and weighed it, measured its density, and named it inflammable air.

His results appeared in 1766 in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions under the plain title Three Papers Containing Experiments on Factitious Air. The name hydrogen came later, coined by Antoine Lavoisier after he repeated Cavendish's experiments and identified the gas as an element in its own right.

Ibn Battuta left Tangier on 14 June 1325, aged twenty one, meaning only to complete the hajj, a pilgrimage to Mecca that usually took sixteen months there and back. He later wrote that an unexplained impulse kept him from turning home once he arrived.

That impulse became three decades on the road through Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula, working along the way as a judge and diplomat. His dictated account, the Rihla, is the reason his roughly 117,000 kilometres of travel are documented at all rather than merely claimed.

ISRO's Mangalyaan probe entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, on a budget of roughly 450 crore rupees, about 74 million US dollars, less than the production cost of some Hollywood space films made the same year. Only the European Space Agency had previously reached Mars orbit on a first attempt; every American and Soviet effort before that had needed at least one failed try.

The spacecraft carried five instruments, none built to survive Mars's radiation for long, yet it kept returning data for over seven years before losing contact in 2022, well past its planned six-month mission. Its propulsion system was designed and built entirely in India, making ISRO the first agency anywhere to reach another planet on home-grown engines.

India detonated five nuclear devices at the Pokhran range in Rajasthan across two days in May 1998, three on the 11th and two more on the 13th, under the codename Operation Shakti. It was India's first test since a single device in 1974, and this time the government declared outright that the country possessed nuclear weapons.

The United States and Japan responded with economic sanctions, and the UN Security Council condemned the tests. Pakistan answered with its own detonations at the end of May, and the two neighbours, already at odds over Kashmir, became the world's newest declared nuclear rivals within the same month.

Ingenuity rose three metres above the floor of Jezero Crater on 19 April 2021, hovered for about forty seconds, and set back down where it started. Its rotors had to spin nearly ten times faster than a helicopter's on Earth to grip an atmosphere just one per cent as dense, and the four-pound machine flew on solar power alone through nights that dropped below minus ninety degrees Celsius.

NASA had planned five test flights to prove powered flight was possible off Earth at all. Ingenuity instead flew seventy two times over nearly three years, covering more than seventeen kilometres and reaching an altitude of twenty four metres, before damage to a rotor blade during a January 2024 landing ended the mission for good.

Frederick Banting and his student assistant Charles Best spent the summer of 1921 in a borrowed University of Toronto laboratory, tying off the pancreatic ducts of dogs so the digestive tissue would wither and leave behind an extract they hoped would control blood sugar. Their supervisor, John Macleod, had been sceptical enough to leave for a holiday in Scotland while they worked.

The biochemist James Collip then purified the extract enough to make it safe for people, and by early 1922 it was being tested on patients in Toronto hospitals. Before this, a diagnosis of severe diabetes meant a slow starvation death within months, and children who had been wasting away began gaining weight and colour within days of the first injections.

Etienne Lenoir's engine of 1859 ran on the same coal gas that lit city streetlamps, drawn in and fired by a spark rather than compressed and ignited like later designs. It had no compression stroke at all, which kept it simple to build but wasted most of the fuel it burned.

It was still the first engine of its kind to sell in any numbers: around 143 had gone to Parisian workshops by 1865, and production reached London too. Fuel consumption ran several times higher than advertised and the engines ran hot and loud, so within a decade more efficient compression designs from rivals such as Nicolaus Otto made it obsolete.

Glass began as beads rather than vessels, and they turn up across Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Syrian coast at roughly the same time, in the mid third millennium BCE. No single workshop can claim the invention: the likeliest path is accidental, a byproduct of metal smelting slag or of firing faience, a glazed ceramic that came first.

Deliberate, sustained glass production took far longer to arrive. Mesopotamia was producing glass in quantity by around 1600 BCE, with Egypt following roughly a century later. Both traditions made small, precious objects, colored beads and inlays rather than clear panes, since transparent glass was still centuries away.

The earliest picture of a sail is not Egyptian. A pottery shard from the Ubaid period in the Persian Gulf, roughly 3500 to 3000 BCE, appears to show a boat with twin masts and a sail, several centuries before any known Egyptian image of one.

Egyptian evidence follows at around 3100 BCE, and it is Egypt's boats on the Nile that are best documented, since sail let a crew travel upstream against the current by catching wind rather than rowing the whole distance. Both regions arrived at the same idea early, and which one used it first is a matter of which shard survived.

Iron working did not begin with a single people or a single breakthrough. Small quantities turn up in Central Anatolia by around 1800 BCE, and separately in the Ganges Valley at about the same date, long before iron replaced bronze anywhere at scale. The idea that the Hittites held a guarded monopoly on the technique has not held up under closer study.

Large-scale iron production only became the norm around 1200 BCE, near the end of the Bronze Age, once smiths learned to forge it into tools stronger and cheaper than cast bronze. The shift mattered most when tin, bronze's scarce ingredient, grew hard to get: iron needed no long-distance trade network, only ore that most regions already had.

Jacquard's 1804 attachment read a chain of punched cards, one per pass of the shuttle. A rod passed freely through each hole; where there was no hole, the rod was pushed aside, lifting or dropping a set of hooks that raised particular warp threads. Swap the deck of cards and the loom wove a different pattern without a weaver touching the threads.

Charles Babbage later planned to store programs for his Analytical Engine on the same kind of card, borrowing the idea directly from Jacquard's loom. Herman Hollerith adapted it again for the 1890 United States census, and punched cards stayed in use for feeding instructions into computers for well over a century afterwards.

An Ariane 5 rocket lifted the James Webb Space Telescope from French Guiana on 25 December 2021, sending it toward a gravitationally stable point 1.5 million kilometres from Earth rather than into orbit around the planet itself, as Hubble had used. Its 6.5-metre segmented mirror, built from eighteen gold-coated hexagons that folded for launch and unfurled in space, gathers about six times the light of Hubble's single 2.4-metre mirror.

Webb observes mostly in infrared rather than visible light, which lets it see through dust clouds and detect galaxies whose light has stretched red over billions of years of travel. That combination lets it pick out objects up to a hundred times fainter than Hubble can manage, reaching back to within roughly 180 million years of the Big Bang.

Japan's earlier Lambda 4S rockets had failed repeatedly to reach orbit, built by the University of Tokyo's Institute of Space and Aeronautical Science rather than a state space agency. On 11 February 1970 the fifth attempt succeeded, carrying the small satellite Ohsumi into orbit.
